idiom_name: lock record row claimed with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE (libpqxx 7 transactions) or BEGIN IMMEDIATE (SQLite)
implementation_notes: The default C++ realization keeps lock records in the same database as the business data: a libpqxx transaction (or the sqlite3 C API) selects the lock row FOR UPDATE, inserts it when absent and updates owner/acquired_at when it is free or expired, then commits immediately so the lease - not the transaction - protects the aggregate. C++ has no ORM to lean on, so this is Fowler's classic structure written by hand; it is still the right form whenever the store supports transactions, because the lock manager can then rely on the engine for the atomic claim.
pitfalls: A lock record row that does not exist yet is not protected by FOR UPDATE: insert-on-missing and update-on-expired must happen inside the same transaction, otherwise two sessions both read 'free'.
Keep the transaction short: a libpqxx work object left alive during user think time holds a connection and its locks, which is exactly what the offline pattern exists to avoid.
SQLite has no row locks, so the sqlite3 flavour uses BEGIN IMMEDIATE and serialises writers - the lock record there is a convention, not an engine-enforced lock.

variants.name: Process-scoped advisory lock on a lock file
variants.idiom_name: Boost.Interprocess file_lock / flock(2) on one lock file per lockable
variants.implementation_notes: For deployments where the store cannot lock rows (embedded databases, shared file stores, or a vendor API with no FOR UPDATE), the lease is a lock file per lockable held by the owner process: Boost.Interprocess file_lock or flock(2) gives an RAII acquire/release that survives individual requests and is dropped automatically when the process dies. It differs from the database variant in where the truth lives - the operating system, not a table - so visibility (who holds what) and timeouts have to be recorded next to it whenever they are needed.
pitfalls: The lease is scoped to the open file/handle: a crash drops it (good for availability, bad if the operation must be resumed) and a leaked RAII object keeps it until the process ends.

Do not use fcntl(F_SETLK) record locks here - they are per-process and are dropped when any descriptor to the file is closed; flock(2) or Boost.Interprocess file locks have per-open-description semantics that model a session better.
Record the owner and acquisition time separately: the operating system will not tell a support engineer who holds a lock or for how long.
